title: What RL on Expert-Built Tasks Teaches Nemotron 3.5 Super
summary: We post-train NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Super (120B total, 12B active parameters) with reinforcement learning (RL) on five expert-built task datasets, one at a time: real-world software engineering, complex constraints, long-horizon tool use, professional chart understanding and enterprise document reasoning. Each run trains a fresh rank-32 LoRA adapter with CISPO on Tinker, with no supervised stage, and each adapter is compared with the base model on the same tasks, harness and settings. On twelve headline benchmarks, eight built by other groups and four by Surge AI, the gains range from +4.5 points on IFBench to +13.8 on GDP_pdf, which rises from 10.4% to 24.2%; SWE-bench Pro V2 rises from 86.9% to 92.1%, Terminal-Bench 2.1 from 63.9% to 70.3%, MultiChallenge from 58.3% to 66.6%, AutomationBench from 14.8% to 27.5% and Chartography from 39.4% to 50.6%. The document adapter, trained without API tools, also gains +8.0 points on AutomationBench. In attempts read side by side with the base model's on tasks each adapter newly solves, the base model's failures recur in a few modes, and each adapter does more often what the base model missed: the tool-use adapter finds the data and the rules before acting, the coding adapter writes its own test or scratch files on SWE-bench Pro V2, the constraints adapter carries earlier turns into its answers, the chart adapter measures the marks in code, and the document adapter reads AutomationBench's spreadsheets.

title: Long-Context Generation Is a Sampling Problem (When You Turn Up the Heat)
summary: Open-weight language models are widely observed to get worse the longer they generate. Often, attempts to fix this involve more training. At high temperature, The sampler, i.e. the rule that picks the next token out of the model's probabilities, decides whether long and agentic generation survives and/or thrives. We test 29 open-weight models from 1B to 122B parameters on ten established benchmarks plus needle retrieval out to one million tokens, covering SWE-bench Verified coding agents, long chain-of-thought reasoning, long-form writing, long structured output and long-context reading. Samplers that keep their pool of candidate tokens small and steady as temperature rises don't lose accuracy. Samplers that let in low-probability tokens fall apart. At temperature 2, coding agents running top-p, top-k or Top-H resolve 0 of 100 GitHub issues, while the same agents running top-nsigma resolve 46 to 62 and win every issue the two samplers disagree on, on three Qwen3.5 models. Over all benchmarks top-nsigma keeps a median 100% of its temperature-1 score where top-p keeps 26%. Counting how many tokens each sampler lets through explains why. In one Llama-3.1-8B story, going from temperature 1 to 2 grows top-p's pool from 4 tokens to 51,845 while top-nsigma stays at 3. Across 133 combinations of sampler setting and temperature, the typical pool size predicts judged quality (Spearman correlation of -0.77), and when we pick the pool at temperature 1 and only apply temperature afterwards, Top-H, min-p and p-less stop collapsing. At the default temperature of 1 most samplers perform about the same, We release all code and data to the public.

title: Weight-Space Programming Doesn't Need Transformers
summary: Standard neural architectures such as the Transformer were chosen because they train well with gradient descent and run fast on GPUs. In weight-space programming, a large language model (LLM) writes target weights by hand without gradient-based training, so those reasons no longer apply. Should we keep the Transformer? Given minimal guidance, ten labeled examples, and a sandbox, mainly on multiple-choice questions, we task three frontier LLMs with either generating the weights of a fixed architecture or designing the architecture themselves. When free to design, all three compile plain-text facts into a sparse table queried by a fixed procedure, reaching up to 54.4% test accuracy. An LLM-designed model achieves higher test accuracy than the most accurate released Transformer that the same LLM wrote while using about 1,800x fewer parameters. Without gradients, they choose a table, in which the LLM can state what each weight means and can find and rewrite a wrong one. Each wrong answer points to one row, and removing a row changes about one other answer. From this, we propose an associative-memory-based model up to 17x faster on GPUs than a same-sized Transformer. We also test pretrained weights, other benchmarks, and tasks where models generate answers. Pretrained LLMs remain more accurate; the claim concerns which structure to build when writing weights.
subject: Computation and Language

title: Thinking Harder Doesn't Lead to Better Choices: Reasoning Effort Increases the Confidence but Not the Correctness of LLM Shopping Agents
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the likelihood it may be wrong? We benchmark ten frontier models on three product-choice benchmarks built from WebShop, Amazon's SQID and Wayfair's WANDS platforms to see if LLMs with more thinking power actually make better-quality product purchase decisions. Across all three benchmarks, we found that increasing the thinking effort does not increase decision quality in a statistically meaningful way. The same change in thinking effort raises stated confidence at a statistically significant level, so extra thinking buys confidence rather than correctness. We also measure the calibration of these models (how well their reported confidence percentage matches their true correctness percentage) in these tasks and show that most models are not well-calibrated at every effort level. We also find that errors are strongly shared: when one model errs in a task, several others tend to err on that same task. Furthermore, on tasks where several models all err, a large number of them pick the same wrong product.
subject: Computation and Language

title: SkillBuffBench: Measuring What Agent Skills Contribute across Harnesses, Models, Skill Access Modes and Memory
summary: Agent Skills, file-based packages of procedural knowledge that a coding agent can discover and load on demand, are now shipped by every major agent harness, yet the evidence for how much they help comes almost entirely from settings in which the right Skill is hand-picked for the task and the agent starts from a blank slate. Neither holds in deployment, where an agent chooses from whatever library happens to be installed and frequently carries memory from earlier work. We present SkillBuffBench, a benchmark and paired evaluation protocol that treats Skill access as a three-level factor (no Skill, a curated Skill, and automatic invocation from an installed library), crosses it with memory (off and on), with four agent harnesses and with multiple models (the state-of-the-art proprietary models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI, and the state-of-the-art open-weight models from Chinese providers), every model being run under every harness, and evaluates the result on research tasks contributed by domain experts together with the Skills they use, currently in materials science and biology, with the suite extended on a rolling basis. Every run is marked by a deterministic verifier; uncertainty is reported with a paired, task-level bootstrap; and cost, agent rounds and wall-clock time are reported alongside the score rather than folded into it. This version of the paper describes the design of the benchmark, its evaluation protocol and its current tasks and Skills. The evaluation is in progress: results will be added once the runs are complete, and the task suite, results and analysis will continue to be updated on a rolling basis.

title: Large Language Models as Nonlinear Dynamical Systems: The Three Clocks of Depth, Training, and Generation
summary: Language models are dynamical systems. A transformer is iterated over its layers, over the steps of its training and over the tokens it generates, and on each of these three clocks it shows behavior that nonlinear dynamics has studied for a century: fixed points, bifurcations, synchronization, chaos and noise-driven escape from potential wells. The two communities rarely meet, so this behavior is often rediscovered under new names. We build a bridge between them. To describe, we condense about 200 papers into the Three-Clock Dictionary, which maps fifteen concepts of nonlinear dynamics onto each clock and marks every correspondence as proved, measured or conjectured, and we show each concept in a mechanical system and in a language model side by side. To explain, we derive reduced-order models: the softmax is a Boltzmann distribution, gradient descent an Euler step on a nonlinear spring, a loss spike a ball thrown out of a stiff valley, attention on the circle a Kuramoto model, and a repetition loop a well that deepens while it is occupied. We then test these explanations on open language models, on a laptop CPU. Escape from repetition loops in GPT-2 and Pythia follows the Arrhenius law with the logit gap as the barrier, and the barrier deepens and then saturates, so the temperature needed to leave a loop falls like $1/\ln N$ with the generation length $N$ and rises with model size. Coherent text lives in a narrow window of temperatures, which a small reasoning model shares at its recommended temperature. Training makes each Pythia layer more expansive, and a small transformer trains at a multi-mode edge of stability. The third step, solving problems of language models, is still ahead: controllers derived from the escape analysis remove loops but do not yet beat the best fixed temperature. We state twelve open problems where nonlinear dynamics could get there.

title: Modeling Document and Section Hierarchies in Embedding Space
summary: Embedded topic models integrate word embeddings into the topic generation process, producing coherent topics and robust performance on large vocabularies. However, each document is represented by a single topic distribution, ignoring its internal structure. Many real world collections, including legal documents, company and government reports, and online discussion forums, exhibit hierarchical organization in which documents consist of multiple sections that often address distinct subtopics. We introduce the Hierarchical Embedded Topic Model (hETM), a structured topic model that couples the topic distribution of a document and those of its sections through a hierarchical prior in the embedding space. We derive an amortized variational inference procedure for hETM and evaluate it on structured collections from each of these domains. Experimental results show that hETM achieves the lowest or near-lowest held-out perplexity among flat and hierarchical topic model baselines, along with comparable or higher topic quality. It also performs strongly on a downstream clustering task, achieving the best clustering performance on most of the collections.
subject: Computation and Language

title: Beyond Bitwidth: Deployment-Constrained Mixed-Precision Quantization for Multilingual LLM Inference on NVIDIA Blackwell
summary: Low-bit LLM quantization is useful only if a model preserves service-relevant accuracy, executes through supported GPU kernels, and meets measured memory and latency limits. We study Qwen3-8B on NVIDIA B200 with vLLM, including INT2/INT3, GPTQ, NVFP4, and mixed-precision configurations. We verify native packed execution and precision on all 144 fused linear modules and evaluate Korean, English, numerical, and reasoning quality under preregistered gates. Packed INT2 and INT3 execute, but all seven tested INT2 grids degenerate on generation. Isolated module-restoration effects are strongly non-additive; Korean and reasoning sensitivity rankings disagree, and a promising INT4/INT8 development candidate fails independent final evaluation. A configuration with 16-bit activations, 98 NVFP4 weight-only modules, 46 INT8 modules, and an INT8 output head passes all gates on the untouched FINAL-81 set (5,168 items): 5.917 GiB of weight-loading memory (limit 5.98), Korean teacher-correct retention 0.904 (gate 0.90), and TPOT ratio 0.939 relative to BF16. It improves paired accuracy over NVFP4 W4A4 by +1.4 percentage points (Bonferroni-adjusted interval [+0.2, +2.6]), compared with +3.4 points on the selection set. This comparison changes both activation precision and INT8 protection; exploratory analyses suggest that the activation change contributes substantially, but the isolated allocation effect is not established. Final checkpoints were not retained, and bitwise rebuild reproducibility remains unverified.
subject: Computation and Language

title: It's My Turn! Interpretable Methods Reveal Developmental Differences from Mother-Child Conversational Dynamics
summary: Understanding conversational interactions between mothers and children is an important challenge for computational behavioral modeling. Existing methods use traditional statistical approaches and subjective measures of conversational dynamics, without incorporating temporal or probabilistic modeling. We developed an interpretable computational framework that combines sequence analysis, information-theoretic measures, and Bayesian hierarchical modeling to characterize temporal conversational dynamics in parent-child play. We applied this framework to interactions from 94 mother-child dyads with two-year-old children. Sequence analysis revealed that dyads with lower language development (as defined by scores on the Bayley developmental test) exhibited more heterogeneous conversational organization and fewer serve-and-return exchanges than higher-development dyads, a reciprocal turn-taking pattern in which one partner initiates communication and the other responds. Mutual information analyses suggested differences in conversational predictability between lower- and higher-development dyads, although the bootstrap confidence intervals overlapped. Bayesian hierarchical models estimated temporal trajectories for maternal consecutive turns, child responses following maternal speech, and overlapping responses; HDIs showed that trajectories differed in whether they excluded 0, but there were no statistically credible differences between the Bayley groups. Overall, these results indicate that children with higher developmental scores have more organized and predictable communication styles, with more ``serve-and-return" patterns with their mothers. These results demonstrate that interpretable computational representations of conversational dynamics capture developmental differences beyond simple measures of speech quantity.
subject: Computation and Language

title: Solver to System: LLM Reasoning Across Representations and Execution in Scientific Simulation
summary: Simulators based on partial differential equations (PDEs) are widely used to model physical systems, but generating and interpreting PDE solver code with large language models (LLMs) remains challenging. Scientific simulation code is a useful testbed for LLM scientific reasoning because (1) one system can be represented by code, equations, natural language, and numerical trajectories and (2) code can execute successfully while implementing invalid physics. We introduce Solver2System, a dataset of PDE solvers with multiple representations, controlled corruptions, and lexical perturbations, to evaluate whether LLMs can recover the underlying physical system through (1) cross-representation consistency and (2) static and agentic detection of physical invalidity. Across eight open-weight models, LLMs systematically favor some representations when evidence conflicts, and lexical perturbations to code alter interpretation of other unchanged representations. Execution improves physical-validity judgments, but weaker agents can judge correctly without identifying the causal defect. Thus, LLMs may reach correct judgments despite inconsistent representation reconciliation or causal misdiagnosis.

title: Conserved Verdicts, Drifting Commitments: Identifying Harmful Overthinking
summary: A reasoning model that has reached a correct answer can lose it by continuing to think. Deciding whether to stop means comparing two probabilities at the same point of a chain: that the answer the model would give if stopped now is correct (its commitment), and that the answer it will finish with is correct (its verdict). We show that the verdict alone, which is what final-correctness probes estimate, cannot make this comparison. As a forecast of a fixed outcome it has no predictable drift, whether continuing helps or hurts. The commitment-verdict gap equals the expected remaining change in answer quality and the accuracy gained by stopping. A second identity splits any accuracy-versus-budget curve into answer change within chains and change in which chains are still running. We measure both on MATH-500. At all 379 points where DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B holds a correct answer, selected without regard to how its chain ends, continuing loses 3.6 points on average (95% CI [2.2, 5.2]), and the loss concentrates in a few problems. In six reasoning models from three families, on MATH-500 and OlympiadBench and with budgets up to 16,384 tokens, declining accuracy curves come from which chains remain, while the chains still reasoning keep or improve their answers. An oracle stopping rule gains at most +1.8 and +2.5 points at 1.5B and 7B. The framework says what to measure before building a stopping rule.
subject: Computation and Language

title: DNeo: Your Parallel Draft Model Needs Better Target Feature Encoding
summary: Speculative-diffusion decoding uses a small parallel drafter model to generate b draft tokens in one forward pass, which then undergo parallel verification via a larger target model. Faster inference can be achieved when multiple draft tokens pass verification simultaneously. Recent parallel draft architectures (DFlash, DSpark) improve draft quality by conditioning on rich features computed by the target, through a mechanism known as feature encoding. However, standard feature encoding mechanisms have three limitations: (1) they are lossy, applying encoding projections that are destructive to the underlying target feature-space via a discovered effect known as residual mixing, (2) they are memory-less, with no record of previously processed proposals, and (3) they utilize features sampled uniformly from across the target layers, omitting important hidden states. To address these issues, we propose Mixture-of-Features Attention (MoFA), a lightweight feature-encoding approach equipped with a working memory that encodes previously rejected proposals. Leveraging MoFA, rejection memory, and a set of further enhancements, including 2-tap causal convolutions, prefix-only cross-attention, and non-uniform target layer selection, the final architecture, DNeo, achieves 1.3x faster generation speed than SoTA (DFlash-2) without impacting drafter footprint or generation quality. DNeo marks a new state of the art in high quality, fast LLM inference.
subject: Computation and Language

title: The Hidden Cost of MoE Diffusion Decoding: Profiling and Fixing the Sampler
summary: Masked diffusion language models (dLLMs) decode by iteratively denoising a full canvas of tokens, so every forward pass runs a per-token sampling and stopping pipeline over the entire canvas-by-vocabulary logits tensor. We profile single-user decoding of a 26B-parameter diffusion Mixture-of-Experts model on a bandwidth-bound edge accelerator (NVIDIA GB10) and report a result that is easy to miss: after weight quantisation, this logits pipeline, not the expert GEMMs, is the single largest consumer of decode time. Unlike autoregressive decoding, where sampling touches one position's logits per committed token, diffusion decoding processes S times as many logit entries per output token, where S is the number of denoising steps. We show this pipeline is largely redundant or fusable and remove it in two lossless tiers: a bit-exact tier whose output is byte-identical to the reference decoder, and an accuracy-parity tier using a fused single-pass entropy kernel and Gumbel-max sampling. Combined with a W4A16 expert kernel, the full stack reaches 2.4-2.7 times end-to-end speedup over bf16 at unchanged benchmark accuracy on GSM8K, HumanEval, and MATH, on a single 273 GB/s device. We confirm the finding on a second, independently built diffusion MoE (LLaDA2.0-mini: pipeline 28.8% of decode, fused W4A16 3.3 times at accuracy parity) and show it disappears on a dense diffusion model (3.6%). The cost is specific to MoE diffusion, where quantisation makes the backbone cheap. Code and quantised weights are released.
subject: Computation and Language

title: Bookkeeping Is Not Judgement: EJBench, an Engineering Judgement Benchmark Built from a Conjugate Heat Transfer Design Campaign
summary: We introduce EJBench, a benchmark of engineering judgement: whether a model can predict how a design behaves at new conditions from a few earlier results, and decide on it. Unlike engineering benchmarks that test whether an agent can operate simulation or CAD software, EJBench is software-agnostic and asks what an engineer would conclude without running a simulation. Its tasks come from a conjugate heat transfer design campaign for battery cold plates, in three families: matching unlabelled test results to their operating points, choosing which stored runs to reveal before signing off a design, and ranking new duties by peak cell temperature. Every answer is taken from a converged simulation, not from an LLM judge. The best of ten frontier models, GPT-6 Astra, scores 0.71, and models state almost the same confidence on tasks they get wrong as on tasks they get right. We also post-train Qwen3.5-9B with LoRA and reinforcement learning, rewarded by the share of answer criteria the simulation results confirm; on the held-out test split its score rises from 0.071 to 0.106. We release the train, validation and test splits, the evaluation harness and the leaderboard.
subject: Computation and Language

title: Watermark Evidence under Open-Weight LLM Modification: Exact Bounds for Low-Rank Output Watermarks
summary: Open-weight language models can continue generating after their released weights are modified, while a watermark verifier still scores outputs against the original base and marked models. We study how such modifications change the evidence available to an OpenStamp-style verifier. At each shared prefix, we represent the modification as a residual in the next-token logits. We derive an exact finite-vocabulary lower bound on the expected log-likelihood-ratio evidence under a residual-span constraint, along with a sharp span-only deviation bound. We also characterize the first-order evidence shift through a covariance term with an explicit second-order remainder, and determine the residual span needed to reach a target evidence level. For sequence-level detection, we derive an exact conditional exponential-moment bound and combine it with a supermartingale argument and a distribution-free order-statistic tolerance bound. This yields a high-confidence upper bound on miss probability after attack selection on calibration data and evaluation on independent certification continuations. In experiments with OpenStamp on Llama-2-7B and Mistral-7B-v0.3, INT8 quantization and 30% pruning retain test true-positive rates of 85.6-94.8%, while 500-step LoRA fine-tuning lowers them to 28.8% and 11.6%. The covariance prediction tracks the measured mean LoRA evidence drift on both models, with no remainder-bound violations across 160,000 test prefixes. Additionally, we observe zero false positives among 500 base-model continuations per model. Through these theoretical and empirical results, the current research provides a better understanding of watermark robustness to model-editing/tuning attacks.
subject: Computation and Language

title: Asking What Matters: Disagreement-Guided Ambiguity Detection for Interactive Text-to-SQL
summary: Interactive text-to-SQL requires an LLM agent not only to generate executable SQL, but also to decide which uncertainty to clarify within a limited interaction budget. However, current clarification policies have three limitations: (i) they target surface ambiguity without testing its SQL impact; (ii) they miss ambiguities implicit in schema routes or domain knowledge; and (iii) they spend limited turns on unfocused or redundant questions. These limitations expose a critical challenge: identifying SQL-impacting ambiguity before the intended SQL is known. In this paper, we propose DisGuAD, a Disagreement-Guided Ambiguity Detection framework that specializes clarification selection. DisGuAD treats disagreement among plausible SQL interpretations as direct evidence of which uncertainty matters to the final query. Specifically, it constructs a query-term inventory, elicits contrastive SQL interpretations through complementary probe families, compares their canonical SQL components, and attributes recurring differences to user-facing clarification targets. A lightweight prioritization and dialogue-state mechanism then selects one high-impact unresolved target for clarification. Experiments on BIRD-Interact Lite and Full with two LLM backbones demonstrate consistent improvements in task success and clarification quality. Compared with the original interaction policy, DisGuAD improves normalized Reward by 4.40--8.97 points and raises overall critical-ambiguity coverage from 48.62% to 82.75% and from 45.76% to 85.14%. Its clarification signals further improve two independently designed static text-to-SQL frameworks by up to 13.97 Reward points while keeping their SQL generators fixed. These results demonstrate that disagreement among plausible SQL queries provides actionable evidence for selecting clarification targets that matter to downstream generation.
subject: Computation and Language

title: ClearTalk: Data-Driven Mandarin Articulation Analysis and Personalized Communication Support for Children with Dysarthria
summary: Children with dysarthria may experience reduced intelligibility and difficulty expressing everyday needs. ClearTalk is a smartwatch-based system that converts Mandarin speech-recognition differences into interpretable articulatory profiles for personalized practice and staged communication. Target and recognized utterances are aligned at the syllable level, summarized across seven articulatory positions, and ranked by a count-sensitive asymmetric heuristic. For 13 dysarthric speakers from the Mandarin Dysarthria Speech Corpus, system syllable-level accuracy showed a Pearson correlation of 0.908 with expert intelligibility, with an R-squared value of 0.824 and a p-value below 0.001. The system-selected priority targets achieved an 86.7 percent overlap with the consensus of three blinded speech-language pathologists; across 210 target consonants, automated labels achieved 86.7 percent agreement, a Cohen's kappa of 0.76, and a macro-F1 score of 0.81. In a balanced single-session pilot with 15 children, mean pre/post gains were 14.4, 29.4, and 27.7 percentage points for mild, moderate, and severe groups, while communication-round completion rates were 81.3, 66.7, and 48.0 percent. These findings support the feasibility of using interpretable patterns of speech errors to guide wearable articulation practice and communication assistance.

title: Label-Wording Augmentation in a Typed-Decision Encoder: Gains on Unfamiliar Words, Not on Abbreviations or Codes
summary: Typed-decision models score options that the caller supplies at request time, so their accuracy depends on label wording that the model's developer does not control. We compare two releases of a 307M-parameter multilingual cross-encoder, Ru-Jev, trained on thirteen Russian-language tasks; the later release adds an augmentation that presents labels in several surface forms. Holding questions fixed and varying only how eighteen routing labels are worded, we evaluate ten label vocabularies at five and eighteen candidates, checked for overlap with the training data. On held-out vocabularies made of ordinary or borrowed words (jargon, office slang, department names), the augmented release has higher point accuracy in all fourteen cells, by up to 0.24. Several of these gains rest partly on one label that the earlier release almost never chose; fitting one bias per option removes part of them, while the jargon gain largely survives. On abbreviations and opaque codes the augmented release gives no usable gain: its loss on 17 abbreviations unrelated to training (-0.060) is one label and disappears after the same correction. The comparison is between two trained releases, not a controlled ablation, and the earlier recipe varies across seeds by up to 0.098 on the strictest slice. On two datasets neither release saw, accuracy moves by -8.4 and +5.6 points, narrowed to -3.4 and +1.4 by the per-option biases; a second training run of each recipe, the augmented one under a rule recorded beforehand, puts the recipe gap on jargon far above seed noise and on a third unseen dataset, scientific rubrics, only just above it. Rankings of training checkpoints disagree across the three unseen datasets, so none of them should choose the checkpoint. We also report four evaluation hazards from comparing the two releases.
subject: Computation and Language

title: Appear2Meaning: A Cross-Cultural Benchmark for Structured Cultural Metadata Inference from Images
authors: Yuechen Jiang, Enze Zhang, Mohsinul Kabir, Chenying Lin, Ying Peng, Fengyuan Liu, Qianqian Xie, Stavroula Golfomitsou, Konstantinos Arvanitis, Sophia Ananiadou
summary: Museum records express how people understand heritage objects through cultural and historical relations. Recovering these human attributions from images is a technical challenge for vision-language models (VLMs). We introduce Appear2Meaning, a cross-cultural benchmark of 750 museum objects for image-only recovery of title, culture, period, origin, and creator. Its evaluation framework distinguishes field-level from complete-record compatibility and uses human validation for semantic judgement. Across nine VLMs, mean field accuracy is 36.16--49.82%; 7.20--17.02% of records have all four contextual fields compatible, and 2.13--7.87% have all five, including title. For the two tested models, image-only input yields 12.6--32.2 percentage points higher reference compatibility for culture, period, and origin than a museum-and-title-only control.
subject: Computation and Language

title: A Multi-Word Tokenizer for 204 Languages That Needs Fewer Tokens Than GPT-4o's, Including on English
authors: Johin Johny Arimbur, Ankur Ashit Ghosh, Shervin Sam
summary: Languages of India need 1.6 to 14 times as many tokens as English on GPT-4o's tokenizer for the same content, which makes them more expensive and slower to serve. We train tokenizers from scratch on human-written text in about 200 languages. Havon v3 is a byte-level BPE tokenizer with 262,144 tokens and a pre-tokenizer that keeps combining marks with their letters and chunks scripts written without spaces. On FLORES-200 devtest it needs fewer tokens than GPT-4o's o200k_base on all 25 languages of India (median 0.74 of GPT-4o's count) and on 172 of 204 languages, but 7% more on English. Havon v4 adds a second, multi-word training stage (SuperBPE) to v3. At exactly GPT-4o's vocabulary size of 200,019 tokens, v4 needs 6.1% fewer tokens than GPT-4o on English and fewer on 161 of 204 languages and all 25 languages of India (median 0.74); at the same size, v3 needs 9.4% more on English and wins on 133. With 262,144 tokens, v4 needs 9.6% fewer tokens on English and fewer on 182 of 204 languages, and with 524,288 tokens it needs fewer on 203 of 204. The gains are largest for English, Hindi and the Romance languages; scripts without spaces, such as Khmer, Burmese and Tibetan, gain little and lose subword merges. Havon v5 replaces v4's Python-only code sample with permissively licensed code in 15 languages: on code it needs 1.03 to 1.22 times GPT-4o's tokens, against 1.11 to 1.29 for v4, while keeping all 25 languages of India (median 0.74, all significant under a sentence-level bootstrap) and English (0.94). These are compression results only: we have not yet evaluated a model trained with v4 or v5.
subject: Computation and Language

title: The Indic Token Tax in 2026: Measuring Tokenizer. Disparity and Its Cost for the Languages of India
authors: Johin Johny Arimbur, Ankur Ashit Ghosh, Shervin Sam
summary: Commercial language model APIs bill per token, so a tokenizer that needs more tokens for the same content in one language makes that language more expensive, slower, and able to fit less text in a fixed context window. We measure this disparity for nine public tokenizers, including those of GPT-4, GPT-4o, Qwen2.5, DeepSeek-V3, Mistral-Nemo and four Sarvam models, on all 25 languages of India available in FLORES-200 (2,009 professionally translated sentences aligned with English) and on 13,732 human-translated Hinglish-English social media pairs from PHINC. On GPT-4o's tokenizer the same content needs between 1.57 times (Hindi) and 5.01 times (Odia) the tokens of English, and 13.7 times for Santali in Ol Chiki script; GPT-4's tokenizer needs up to 12.8 times. Sarvam-30B/105B is the only third-party tokenizer that stays below 2.6 times on every language (median 1.53). In an illustrative scenario using official list prices accessed on 5 November 2026 and stated assumptions, a support bot handling 100,000 chats a month on GPT-4o would cost about INR 56,640 in English and INR 102,829 in Marathi; these are estimates, not measured production costs. Against an openly licensed Hindi and Marathi morphological segmentation set, no tokenizer places more than 35% of its word-internal boundaries on morpheme boundaries (boundary F1 at most 0.48). In a companion paper we present a tokenizer that reduces this tax. Code, pinned artifacts and raw token counts are available at https://github.com/HavonAI/indic-token-tax.
subject: Computation and Language

title: Multilingual Hallucination Gaps in Large Language Models
authors: Cl\'ea Chataigner, Afaf Ta\"ik, Golnoosh Farnadi
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as alternatives to traditional search engines given their capacity to generate text that resembles human language. However, this shift is concerning, as LLMs often generate hallucinations, misleading or false information that appears highly credible. In this study, we explore the phenomenon of hallucinations across multiple languages in freeform text generation, focusing on what we call multilingual hallucination gaps. These gaps reflect differences in the frequency of hallucinated answers depending on the prompt and language used. To quantify such hallucinations, we used the FactScore metric and extended its framework to a multilingual setting. We conducted experiments using LLMs from the LLaMA, Qwen, and Aya families, generating biographies in 19 languages and comparing the results to Wikipedia pages. Our results reveal variations in hallucination rates, especially between high and low resource languages, raising important questions about LLM multilingual performance and the challenges in evaluating hallucinations in multilingual freeform text generation.
subject: Computation and Language

title: Hallucination Mitigation using Agentic AI Natural Language-Based Frameworks
summary: Hallucinations remain a significant challenge for Generative AI, undermining trust in AI systems and their reliability. This study investigates how orchestrating multiple specialized AI agents can mitigate hallucinations, with a focus on systems that use Natural Language Processing (NLP) for agent interaction. We design a pipeline that feeds 310 prompts, purposefully crafted to induce hallucinations, into a front-end agent; its outputs are reviewed and refined by second- and third-level agents that detect unverified claims, add explicit disclaimers and clarify speculative content. We introduce four novel Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) - Factual Claim Density, Factual Grounding References, Fictional Disclaimer Frequency and Explicit Contextualization Score - aggregated into a Total Hallucination Score (THS) and assessed by a dedicated fourth-level evaluator agent. Inter-agent context is carried by the Open Floor Protocol (OFP, formerly OVON, Open Voice Network), whose structured JSON messages let each reviewer pass its assessment of hallucination likelihood, and the reasons behind it, to the next stage. Across the 310 prompts, THS improves by a mean of -0.131 per prompt from the front-end agent to the final reviewer (Cohen's d = 2.38), with lower scores on 302 of 310 prompts. The gain is carried mainly by explicit disclaimers and contextualization, making speculative content more transparent and clearly demarcated from factual claims. The results show that multi-agent orchestration with structured, NLP-based exchange of meta-information can substantially strengthen the epistemic framing of AI-generated responses and improve their explainability.
subject: Computation and Language

title: 3D-MoE: Towards Spatial Intelligence with Mixture-of-Experts for 3D Reasoning and Action Generation
authors: Yueen Ma, Zenglin Xu, Irwin King
summary: Spatial intelligence, encompassing 3D perception and reasoning, is the essential next frontier of AI. Scaling current 3D vision-language models (VLMs) that rely on dense Transformers for spatial tasks incurs prohibitive computational costs. In this paper, we introduce 3D-MoE, a 3D VLM leveraging an efficient mixture-of-experts architecture with a modality- and spatial-context-aware probabilistic routing scheme, stably cultivated by a novel routing curriculum. To seamlessly extend 3D-MoE to embodied AI, we integrate a diffusion-based action head, Pose-DiT, transforming 3D-MoE into a 3D vision-language-action (VLA) model. By employing a rectified flow framework, Pose-DiT generates precise 6D pose actions in a single sampling step. Extensive experiments demonstrate that 3D-MoE achieves superior performance on diverse 3D vision-language benchmarks with drastically fewer activated parameters and yields higher success rates while enabling real-time inference for robot manipulation tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/yueen-ma/3D-MoE.
subject: Computation and Language

title: Breaking the Silence: A Dataset and Benchmark for Bangla Text-to-Gloss Translation
authors: Sharif Mohammad Abdullah, Abhijit Paul, Shubhashis Roy Dipta, Zarif Masud, Shebuti Rayana, Ahmedul Kabir
summary: Gloss is a written approximation that bridges Sign Language (SL) and its corresponding spoken language. Despite a deaf and hard-of-hearing population of at least 3 million in Bangladesh, Bangla Sign Language (BdSL) remains largely understudied, with very limited prior work on Bangla text-to-gloss translation and no publicly available parallel dataset at the time of this work. To address this gap, we construct the first publicly available Bangla text-to-gloss dataset, consisting of 1,000 manually annotated and 4,000 synthetically generated Bangla sentence-gloss pairs, along with 159 expert human-annotated pairs used as a test set. Our experimental framework performs a comparative analysis between several fine-tuned open-source models and a leading closed-source LLM to evaluate their performance in low-resource BdSL translation. GPT-5.4 achieves the best automatic metric scores, while open-source models perform competitively despite being much smaller. This work introduces the first publicly available expert-annotated Bangla text-to-gloss dataset, benchmark and trained model for Bangla text-to-gloss translation. It also demonstrates the effectiveness of systematically generated synthetic data for addressing challenges in low-resource sign language translation.
subject: Computation and Language

title: Semiotic Complexity and Its Epistemological Implications for Modeling Culture
authors: Zachary K. Stine, James E. Deitrick
summary: Greater theorizing of methods in the computational humanities is needed for epistemological and interpretive clarity, and therefore the maturation of the field. In this paper, we frame such modeling work as engaging in translation work from a cultural, linguistic domain into a computational, mathematical domain, and back again. Translators benefit from articulating the theory of their translation process, and so do computational humanists in their work -- to ensure internal consistency, avoid subtle yet consequential translation errors, and facilitate interpretive transparency. Our contribution in this paper is to lay out a particularly consequential dimension of the lack of theorizing and the sorts of translation errors that emerge in our modeling practices as a result. Along these lines we introduce the idea of semiotic complexity as the degree to which the meaning of some text may vary across interpretive lenses, and make the case that dominant modeling practices -- especially around evaluation -- commit a translation error by treating semiotically complex data as semiotically simple when it seems epistemologically convenient by conferring superficial clarity. We then lay out several recommendations for researchers to better account for these epistemological issues in their own work.
subject: Computation and Language

title: PersonaFuse: A Situation-Aware Post-Training Framework for Adaptive LLM Behavior in Enterprise Tasks
authors: Yixuan Tang, Yi Yang, Ahmed Abbasi
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in enterprise settings to support task execution and workflow automation. Despite the strong performance of general-purpose models on standard benchmarks, organizations often need to adapt them to domain-specific tasks and operational constraints in practice. However, existing post-training approaches introduce capability trade-offs and lack mechanisms for situational adaptation. In this work, we propose PersonaFuse, a post-training framework that enables situation-aware behavioral adaptation in LLMs. Grounded in Trait Activation Theory and operationalized through the Five-Factor Model, PersonaFuse dynamically adjusts model behavior based on task context using a mixture-of-experts architecture with trait-level experts and a context-aware routing mechanism. We evaluate PersonaFuse at three levels. At the capability level, it achieves balanced improvements across general reasoning, interaction quality, and safety without introducing trade-offs. At the workflow level, it improves task completion in enterprise scenarios involving tool use and structured execution across both B2B and B2C tasks. At the deployment level, we analyze model selection under cost and safety constraints using a capability-cost frontier framework, showing that models adapted with PersonaFuse achieve more favorable trade-offs and are consistently selected as optimal across deployment scenarios. PersonaFuse provides a practical framework for developing LLMs that are not only capable, but also adaptable and deployable in real-world enterprise environments.
subject: Computation and Language

title: Feedback Forensics: A Toolkit to Measure AI Personality
authors: Arduin Findeis, Timo Kaufmann, Eyke H\"ullermeier, Robert Mullins
summary: Some traits making a "good" AI model are hard to describe upfront. For example, should responses be more polite or more casual? Such traits are sometimes summarized as model character or personality. Without a clear objective, conventional benchmarks based on automatic checks struggle to measure such traits. Evaluation methods using human feedback such as Chatbot Arena have emerged as a popular alternative. These methods infer "better" personality and other desirable traits implicitly by ranking multiple model responses relative to each other. Recent issues with model releases highlight limitations of these existing opaque evaluation approaches: goblin-obsessed, sycophantic and generally over-the-top personalities have resulted in model rollbacks and extensive media coverage. Despite these known issues, limited public tooling exists to explicitly evaluate model personality. We introduce Feedback Forensics: an open-source toolkit to track AI personality and related behavioural traits, both those encouraged by human (or AI) feedback, and those exhibited across AI models trained and evaluated on such feedback. Feedback Forensics is adaptive and can automatically find new traits appearing in models. We demonstrate the toolkit's usefulness in two steps: (A) first we analyse the personality traits encouraged in popular human feedback datasets including MultiPref, PRISM and data from Chatbot Arena; and (B) then use our toolkit to analyse how much popular models exhibit such traits. We release (1) our Feedback Forensics toolkit alongside (2) a web app tracking AI personality in popular models and feedback datasets and (3) the underlying annotation data, see https://github.com/rdnfn/feedback-forensics.
subject: Computation and Language

title: Beating Hateful Narratives on Social Media with Facts: Retrieval-Augmented Counter-Speech Generation
authors: Greta Damo, Elena Cabrio, Serena Villata
summary: Online hate speech threatens social cohesion by amplifying discrimination and harmful narratives against marginalized communities. While counter-speech (CS) - fact-based, respectful responses to hate - offers a constructive alternative to content removal, its large-scale generation remains constrained by factual reliability and the risk of generic responses. We address these challenges with a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline grounded in the first large-scale, curated knowledge base built from authoritative international and regional human rights sources, including the United Nations Digital Library, EUR-Lex, and the EU Agency for Fundamental Rights. The framework covers eight groups frequently targeted by online abuse. We systematically evaluate all pipeline components demonstrating that each design choice is empirically motivated, combining automatic metrics, LLM-based judgments, and human evaluation with comparisons against strong baselines. Results show that RAG improves factual grounding, diversity, and perceived effectiveness over No-RAG and performs favorably against existing systems. Our human evaluation further reveals differences between in-group and out-group perceptions of CS, with RAG narrowing but not eliminating this gap. These findings highlight the potential of knowledge grounded CS for scalable social media interventions, while underscoring the need to evaluate such systems with and for the communities they are intended to serve.
subject: Computation and Language

title: Readers Prefer Outputs of AI Trained on Copyrighted Books over Expert Human Writers
authors: Tuhin Chakrabarty, Jane C. Ginsburg, Paramveer Dhillon
summary: The use of copyrighted books for training AI has sparked lawsuits from authors concerned about AI generating derivative content. Yet whether these models can produce high-quality literary text emulating authors' voices remains unclear. We conducted a preregistered study comparing MFA-trained writers with three frontier models (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini) writing up to 450-word excerpts emulating 50 award-winning authors' styles. In blind pairwise evaluations by 28 MFA-trained readers and 516 college-educated general readers, AI text from in-context prompting was strongly disfavored by MFA readers for stylistic fidelity (OR=0.16) and quality (OR=0.13), while general readers showed no fidelity preference (OR=1.06) but favored AI for quality (OR=1.82). Fine-tuning ChatGPT on authors' complete works reversed these results: MFA readers favored AI for fidelity (OR=8.16) and quality (OR=1.87), with general readers showing even stronger preference (fidelity OR=16.65; quality OR=5.42). Both groups preferred fine-tuned AI, but the writer-type X reader-type interaction remained significant (p=0.021 for fidelity; p<10^-4 for quality), indicating general readers favored AI by a wider margin. Effects are robust under cluster-robust inference and generalize across authors in heterogeneity analyses. Fine-tuned outputs were rarely flagged as AI-generated (3% vs. 97% for prompting) by leading detectors. Mediation analysis shows fine-tuning eliminates detectable AI quirks that penalize in-context outputs, altering the nexus between detectability and preference. While not accounting for effort to transform AI output into publishable prose, the median fine-tuning cost of $81 per author represents a 99.7% reduction versus typical writer compensation. Author-specific fine-tuning enables non-verbatim AI writing preferred over expert human writing, providing evidence relevant to copyright's fourth fair-use factor.
subject: Computation and Language

title: Guideline-Based Medical Reasoning in LLMs
authors: Michael Staniek, Artem Sokolov, Stefan Riezler
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at medical question-answering, yet progress toward medical reasoning models is limited by the lack of scalable, trustworthy reasoning supervision. We propose tapping into the so far underused resource of medical consensus guidelines. These map numerical clinical measurements to disease scores and can optionally be curated for site-specific exceptions. Automatically generating gold-standard reasoning chains from consensus rules enables both large-scale supervised fine-tuning and automatic evaluation. Applying SOFA, SAPS-II, and Sepsis-3 guidelines to MIMIC-III, we show that small fine-tuned models significantly outperform larger one-shot prompted models in derivation correctness and F1 score, achieving near-perfect deductive inference and reliable exception handling. Trustworthy step-by-step reasoning does not reliably emerge from one-shot prompting, even when models receive the consensus definition and an example. Performance across all models declines when forecasting future clinical variables, indicating that, on the evaluated structured ICU tasks, the central challenge is not rule application, but the orthogonal problem of generalizing into the future for prognostic reasoning.
subject: Computation and Language

title: Adapting Large Language Models to Low-Resource Tibetan: A Two-Stage Continual and Supervised Fine-Tuning Study
authors: Lifeng Chen, Chenyang Zhong, Ryan Lai, Tianming Liu
summary: Adapting large language models (LLMs) to low-resource languages remains a major challenge due to data scarcity and cross-lingual drift. This work presents a two-stage adaptation of Qwen2.5-3B to Tibetan, a morphologically rich and underrepresented language. We employ Continual Pretraining (CPT) to establish Tibetan linguistic grounding, followed by Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) for task and translation specialization. Empirical evaluations demonstrate a consistent decrease in perplexity (from 2.98 $\rightarrow$ 1.54) and substantial improvements in Chinese$\rightarrow$Tibetan translation quality (BLEU: 0.046 $\rightarrow$ 0.261; chrF: 2.2 $\rightarrow$ 6.6). Layer-wise analysis across 435 layers in Qwen3-4B reveals that adaptation primarily concentrates on embedding and output heads, with mid--late MLP projections encoding domain-specific transformations. Our findings suggest that CPT constructs a Tibetan semantic manifold while SFT sharpens task alignment with minimal representational disruption. This study provides the first quantitative exploration of Tibetan adaptation dynamics for LLMs, and offers an open, reproducible framework for extending multilingual foundation models to low-resource settings.
subject: Computation and Language

title: From Evidence to Judgment: Trace-Augmented Reasoning under Conflicting Evidence
authors: Shubham Mishra, Atharv Sharma, Dhruv Kumar, Harsh Sharma
summary: Retrieved documents often disagree, contain outdated information, or fail to support any answer, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems have no reliable way to decide which documents to trust. We treat this as a reasoning problem and test it separately from answer generation. We release 943 training and validation examples and a disjoint 736-example benchmark, and fine-tune four language models to write a structured think trace before answering: the model judges each document, infers the conflict pattern, and writes a grounded answer or a justified refusal. Our evaluation framework, CATS (Conflict-Aware Trust Score), scores grounded refusal, behavioural adherence, factual grounding, and single-truth recall; a human study validates factual grounding and single-truth recall (kappa=0.78 and 0.79). The think trace improves the answer/refuse decision: under all three prompts, untuned models score at most 0.429 Refusal F1 (F1 with refusal as the positive class) and trace-tuned models at least 0.826. On the answerable examples a model answers, factual grounding under the 40-word prompt is at most 0.11 for untuned and 0.86-0.88 for trace-tuned models. Cutting the prompt from 1,965 words to 40 leaves trace-tuned scores within the benchmark's measurement noise (+/-0.034). Answer-only fine-tuning trails trace supervision on every metric under the minimal prompt.
subject: Computation and Language

title: CD4LM: Consistency Distillation and aDaptive Decoding for Diffusion Language Models
authors: Yihao Liang, Ze Wang, Ximeng Sun, Jiang Liu, Jialian Wu, Hao Chen, Xiaodong Yu, Emad Barsoum, Zicheng Liu, Niraj K. Jha
summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) accelerate generation by decoding multiple tokens in parallel, but pushing them to fast decoding often sacrifices accuracy. We attribute this to a static-to-dynamic mismatch: training optimizes local denoising under fixed schedules, while fast inference skips steps and encounters irregular mask patterns. Existing accelerators largely address only one side of this problem. Training-free inference methods speed up decoding without changing the model, leaving the mismatch unresolved; training-side distillation methods adapt the model, but often tie the student to a specific decoding trajectory, limiting composability and still suffering accuracy loss. We propose CD4LM, a composable framework for accurate DLM acceleration. Its core training component, Discrete-Space Consistency Distillation (DSCD) trains a trajectory-invariant student on diverse masked states, reducing the mismatch without fixing a decoding policy. We pair DSCD with a lightweight ConfidenceAdaptive Decoder, while keeping the trained student compatible with external inference-side accelerators. On GSM8K, CD4LM preserves accuracy while achieving a 5.18x speedup; stacking CD4LM with per-step cache accelerators further pushes speedup to 9.73x at teacher-level accuracy, suggesting a scalable path for combining training-side robustness with future decoding advances. Code is available at https://github.com/yihao-liang/CDLM.
subject: Computation and Language

title: Why Steering Works: Toward a Unified View of Language Model Parameter Dynamics
authors: Ziwen Xu, Chenyan Wu, Hengyu Sun, Haiwen Hong, Mengru Wang, Yunzhi Yao, Longtao Huang, Hui Xue, Shumin Deng, Zhixuan Chu, Huajun Chen, Ningyu Zhang
summary: Methods for controlling large language models (LLMs), including local weight fine-tuning, LoRA-based adaptation, and activation-based interventions, are often studied in isolation, obscuring their connections and making comparison difficult. In this work, we present a unified view that frames these interventions as dynamic weight updates induced by a control signal, placing them within a single conceptual framework. Building on this view, we propose a unified preference-utility analysis that separates control effects into preference, defined as the tendency toward a target concept, and utility, defined as coherent and task-valid generation, and measures both on a shared log-odds scale using polarity-paired contrastive examples. Across methods, we observe a consistent trade-off between preference and utility: stronger control increases preference while predictably reducing utility. We further explain this behavior through an activation manifold perspective, in which control shifts representations along target-concept directions to enhance preference, while utility declines primarily when interventions push representations off the model's valid-generation manifold. Finally, we introduce a new steering approach SPLIT guided by this analysis that improves preference while better preserving utility. Code is available at https://github.com/zjunlp/EasyEdit/blob/main/examples/SPLIT.md.
subject: Computation and Language

title: How Controllable Are Large Language Models? A Unified Evaluation across Behavioral Granularities
authors: Ziwen Xu, Kewei Xu, Haoming Xu, Haiwen Hong, Longtao Huang, Hui Xue, Ningyu Zhang, Yongliang Shen, Guozhou Zheng, Huajun Chen, Shumin Deng
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in socially sensitive domains, yet their unpredictable behaviors, ranging from misaligned intent to inconsistent personality, pose significant risks. We introduce SteerEval, a hierarchical benchmark for evaluating LLM controllability across three domains: language features, sentiment, and personality. Each domain is structured into three specification levels: L1 (what to express), L2 (how to express), and L3 (how to instantiate), connecting high-level behavioral intent to concrete textual output. Using SteerEval, we systematically evaluate contemporary steering methods, revealing that control often degrades at finer-grained levels. Our benchmark offers a principled and interpretable framework for safe and controllable LLM behavior, serving as a foundation for future research.
subject: Computation and Language

title: A Parameter-Efficient Transfer Learning Approach through Multitask Prompt Distillation and Decomposition for Clinical NLP
authors: Cheng Peng, Mengxian Lyu, Ziyi Chen, Yonghui Wu
summary: Existing prompt-based fine-tuning methods typically learn task-specific prompts independently, imposing significant computing and storage overhead at scale when deploying multiple clinical natural language processing (NLP) systems. We present a multitask prompt distillation and decomposition framework that learns a single shared metaprompt from 21 diverse clinical source tasks and adapts it to unseen target tasks with fewer than 0.05% trainable parameters. Evaluated across five clinical NLP task types (named entity recognition, relation extraction, question answering, natural language inference, and summarization) on 10 held-out target datasets using three backbone models (LLaMA 3.1 8B, Meditron3 8B, gpt-oss 20B), our framework consistently outperforms LoRA by 1.5~1.7% despite using orders of magnitude fewer parameters, and exceeds single-task prompt tuning by 6.1~6.6%. The gpt-oss 20B model achieves the highest overall performance, particularly on clinical reasoning tasks. The strong zero- and few-shot performance demonstrates better transferability of the shared prompt representation.
subject: Computation and Language

title: Verbal tics in frontier language models: A critical review of current releases, research evidence, and public discussion
authors: Shuai Wu, Xue Li, Zhijun Wang, Bolun Liu, Weilin Cai, Zihao Su, Ran Wang
summary: Repeated praise, canned reassurance, formulaic contrasts, and conspicuous vocabulary figure prominently in discussions of large language models. Context governs how these habits should be read. A conventional phrase can orient a reader, whereas a fluent answer can reinforce a false belief. This critical review examines linguistic habits and sycophancy across eight developer families. We verify public offerings from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, xAI, ByteDance, Moonshot AI, DeepSeek, and Xiaomi against official release and API documentation through 1 October 2026. We then synthesize empirical research on lexical overrepresentation, stylistic variation, social warmth, and agreement alongside benchmark methods and dated public discussions in English and Chinese. Published studies document recurring linguistic patterns and agreement that distorts human judgment, but comparable measurements for the newest releases remain sparse in the retrieved material. Current user accounts report both persistent complaints and clearer prose, and experiences vary by task and prompt design. We propose separate measures for recurrence, contextual appropriateness, and belief distortion paired with exact service records and language-specific annotation. This framework keeps claims about writing quality and conversational reliability testable as model services change.
subject: Computation and Language

title: Seeing Is No Longer Believing: Frontier Image Generation Models, Synthetic Visual Evidence, and Real-World Risk
authors: Shuai Wu, Xue Li, Zhijun Wang, Bolun Liu, Weilin Cai, Zihao Su, Ran Wang
summary: Image generation systems can produce plausible photographs, readable documents, and consistent depictions of people and places. Presented as records of real events, these outputs can influence decisions in news, finance, identity verification, medicine, and law. This narrative review examines public model documentation, incident reports, empirical studies, governance materials, and illustrative English and Chinese practitioner commentary available through 1 October 2026. We separate vendor capability claims, documented incidents, experimental findings, and prospective harm pathways. Realism, text rendering, reference consistency, conversational editing, search grounding, and low generation cost shape the conditions under which synthetic images acquire evidentiary weight. Documented episodes show how fabricated visuals enter public and institutional workflows, although public reporting cannot measure misuse prevalence for current releases. Comparing provider safeguards, provenance credentials, watermarks, platform labels, and statutory duties shows that origin signals do not verify a depicted event or transaction. Our framework matches artifact types and decision stakes to specific controls. Consequential decisions require authenticated source records, independent channel corroboration, and proportionate review before action.
subject: Computation and Language

title: Fuzzy Fingerprinting Encoder Pre-trained Language Models for Emotion Recognition in Conversations: Human Assessment and Validity Study
authors: Patr\'icia Pereira, Helena Moniz, Joao Paulo Carvalho
summary: In Emotion Recognition in Conversations (ERC), model decisions should align with nuanced human perception and ideally provide insights on the classification process. Standard encoder pre-trained language models (PLMs) are the state-of-the-art at these tasks but offer little insight into why a certain prediction is made. This is especially problematic in imbalanced datasets, where most utterances are labeled as neutral, making these models frequently misclassify minority emotions as the majority neutral class. To tackle this issue, we introduced a novel, interpretable approach to ERC by combining PLMs with Fuzzy Fingerprints (FFPs). FFP provide class-specific prototypes that reflect the characteristic class activation patterns in the PLM's latent space. They are derived by ranking and fuzzifying the activations of the pooled conversational context-dependent embeddings across training instances for each emotion. At inference time, each input utterance is similarly fuzzy fingerprinted and matched to the emotion prototypes using a fuzzy similarity function based on the aggregation of the intersection of the fuzzy sets that define each FFP. Experimental results show that FFP integration reduces overclassification into the neutral class and human evaluation further supports the adequacy of FFP predictions. Our proposed method thus bridges the gap between deep neural inference and human perception, performing at state-of-the-art level while simultaneously offering valuable insights into the classification procedure.
subject: Computation and Language

title: The First Token Knows: Single-Decode Confidence for Hallucination Detection
summary: Sampling-based uncertainty methods detect hallucinations by generating multiple answers and measuring agreement, often with additional semantic clustering. We study whether uncertainty is already visible in the first content-bearing answer token of a single greedy decode. We define first-token confidence, phi_first, as one minus the normalized entropy of the top-K first-token distribution. Across PopQA and TriviaQA with three 7-8B instruction-tuned models, phi_first matches or modestly exceeds semantic self-consistency while requiring only one decode instead of one greedy decode plus ten sampled generations and NLI clustering. A subsumption analysis shows that phi_first is moderately to strongly correlated with semantic agreement, and combining both signals yields only small additional AUROC gains. We position phi_first as a cheap deployment-oriented baseline for factual QA uncertainty estimation, while noting its limits for high-confidence falsehoods and long-form generation.
subject: Computation and Language

title: The Metacognitive Profile Atlas: Domain-level confidence discrimination in 33 frontier LLMs on MMLU
summary: We release the Metacognitive Profile Atlas, a corpus of answer-plus-verbalized-confidence data from 33 frontier LLMs on 1,500 MMLU items stratified into six subject-group bins (46,157 scored observations after excluding parser-supplied values). The data allow Type-2 AUROC, the degree to which confidence discriminates correct from incorrect answers, to be decomposed by domain. The reliable finding is a population-level ordering on MMLU. Confidence discriminates best on Applied/Professional items (mean AUROC .750; ranked first in 100% of bootstrap resamples) and worst on Formal Reasoning and Natural Science (bottom two in 93% and 92%; Friedman chi^2(5) = 28.26, p < .0001). After Holm correction Applied exceeds Formal, Science, Social and Humanities; no other pair survives, including Applied versus Factual. The ordering holds when imprecise cells are excluded or down-weighted. Per-model six-domain profiles are not reliable (median split-half r = .16) and are released for exploration only; the six bins are a pragmatic grouping, not a latent construct. Within-family similarity of profile shape is significant overall, but after multiplicity correction only Anthropic is individually supported. Paired-item analysis separates genuine monitoring gains (Opus 4.1 to 4.5 and 4.7) from error removal (Gemma 3 27B to Gemma 4 31B). Models whose binary-probe confidence failed or could not be certified on a separate battery discriminate well under verbalized confidence, and three Gemma 3 models show the reverse pattern. This version incorporates revisions committed during peer review, corrects descriptions of external validity-screen results, and excludes 980 parser-imputed confidence values for GPT-oss-120B, whose v1 profile was an artefact of them.
subject: Computation and Language

title: SimCT: Recovering Lost Supervision for Cross-Tokenizer On-Policy Distillation
authors: Jie Sun, Mao Zheng, Mingyang Song, Qiyong Zhong, Yilin Cheng, Bichuan Feng, Pengfei Liu, Junfeng Fang, Xiang Wang
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a standard tool for transferring teacher behavior to a smaller student, but it implicitly assumes that teacher and student predictions are comparable token by token, an assumption that fails whenever the two models tokenize the same text differently. Under heterogeneous tokenizers, exact shared-token matching silently discards a large fraction of the teacher signal at precisely the positions where vocabularies disagree. We propose \textbf{\underline{Sim}ple \underline{C}ross-\underline{T}okenizer OPD (SimCT)}, which restores this signal by enlarging the supervision space: alongside shared tokens, SimCT compares teacher and student over short multi-token continuations that both tokenizers can realize, leaving the OPD loss form itself unchanged. We show that these units are the finest jointly tokenizable supervision interface, and that coarser alternatives remove teacher-student distinctions that are useful for on-policy learning. Across three heterogeneous teacher-student pairs on mathematical reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, SimCT shows consistent gains over shared-vocabulary OPD and representative cross-tokenizer baselines, with ablations confirming that the improvements come from recovering supervision discarded by exact shared-token matching. Code is available at \href{https://github.com/sunjie279/SimCT-}{https://github.com/sunjie279/SimCT-}.
subject: Computation and Language

title: Test-Time Speculation
authors: Avinash Kumar, Sujay Sanghavi, Poulami Das
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference by using a fast draft model to generate tokens and a more accurate target model to verify them. Its performance depends on the $\textit{acceptance length}$, or number of draft tokens accepted by the target. Our studies show that the acceptance length of even state-of-the-art speculators, like DFlash, EAGLE-3, and PARD, degrades with generation length, reaching values close to 1 (i.e., no speedup) within a few thousand output tokens, making speculators ineffective for long-response tasks. Acceptance lengths decline because most speculators are trained offline on short sequences, but are forced to match the target on much longer outputs at inference, well beyond their training distribution. To address this issue, we propose $\textit{Test-Time Speculation (TTS)}$, an online distillation approach that continuously adapts the speculator at test time. TTS leverages the key insight that the token verification step already invokes the target model for each draft token, providing the training signal needed to adapt the draft at no additional cost. Treating the draft as the student and the target as the teacher, TTS adjusts the draft over several speculation rounds, with each update improving the draft's accuracy as generation proceeds. Our results across ten models from the Qwen-3, Qwen-3.5, DeepSeek-R1, GPT-OSS, MiniMax, and Llama3.1 families show that TTS improves acceptance lengths over state-of-the-art speculators by up to $72\%$ and $41\%$ on average, with the benefits scaling with generation lengths.
subject: Computation and Language

title: Inducing Artificial Uncertainty in Language Models
authors: Sophia Hager, Simon Zeng, Nicholas Andrews
summary: In safety-critical applications, language models should be able to characterize their uncertainty with meaningful probabilities. Many uncertainty quantification approaches require supervised data; however, finding suitable unseen challenging data is increasingly difficult for large language models trained on vast amounts of scraped data. If the model is consistently (and correctly) confident in its predictions, the uncertainty quantification method may consistently overestimate confidence on new and unfamiliar data. Finding data which exhibits enough uncertainty to train supervised uncertainty quantification methods for high-performance models may therefore be challenging, and will increase in difficulty as LLMs saturate datasets. To address this issue, we first introduce the problem of inducing artificial uncertainty in language models, then investigate methods of inducing artificial uncertainty on trivially easy data in the absence of challenging data at training time. We use probes trained to recognize artificial uncertainty on the original model, and find that these probes trained on artificial uncertainty outperform probes trained without artificial uncertainty in recognizing real uncertainty, achieving notably higher calibration on hard data with minimal loss of performance on easy data.
subject: Computation and Language

title: Harmony in Diversity: Multi-domain Contrastive Policy Optimization for Large Reasoning Models
authors: Zongji Yu, Wenshui Luo, Yiliu Sun, Hao Fang, Hanrui Xu, Runmin Cong, Chaochao Lu, Chen Gong
summary: Multi-domain capabilities are critical for practically applicable Large Reasoning Models (LRMs). Therefore, mixed-domain Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a crucial process to jointly train a single LRM with mixed domain data, but it often induces capability trade-offs among different domains. Existing methods attribute this issue to competing cross-domain interactions, and mitigate them by isolating learning directions and balancing learning progress. However, our observation suggests that they also impede supportive knowledge sharing across domains, which make it difficult to match or surpass single-domain performance. To address this problem, we propose \textbf{M}ulti-domain \textbf{C}ontrastive \textbf{P}olicy \textbf{O}ptimization (MCPO), which applies contrastive learning to achieve diverse knowledge sharing and competition. We first localize the interaction units on critical reasoning segments, and then formulate mutually augmented examples to capture both positive and negative interactions. Subsequently, we design complementary contrastive objectives for cross-domain knowledge sharing and intra-domain knowledge consolidation. Overall, we utilize diverse cross-domain interactions to achieve compatibility across domains and discriminability within each domain to form a harmonious reasoning space. Experimental results across a broad range of domains show that MCPO significantly outperforms existing methods mitigating interactions over 3.17 average points, and even surpasses single-domain training over 1.05 average points.
subject: Computation and Language

title: JuICE: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLM-Judge in Identifying Cultural Errors
authors: Jiho Jin, Junho Myung, Juhyun Oh, Junyeong Park, Rifki Afina Putri, Sunipa Dev, Vinodkumar Prabhakaran, Alice Oh
summary: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed to users around the world, they are integrated into everyday tasks across diverse cultural contexts, from drafting personal communications to brainstorming creative ideas. These tasks are inherently cultural: they require contextual appropriateness, symbolic resonance, and tacit cultural expectations that native speakers draw on instinctively, meaning that a response can be factually plausible yet unmistakably wrong to a local reader. Existing cultural benchmarks have treated culture as a flat set of facts via fact verification or norm entailment methods, and have adopted LLM-as-a-Judge without examining whether they can capture such thick cultural errors. To address this gap, we present JuICE (Benchmark for LLM-Judge in Identifying Cultural Errors), a multilingual dataset of 7,470 span-level annotations of cultural and linguistic errors in long-form LLM responses. It covers 1,050 query-response pairs from four countries (the United States, South Korea, Indonesia, and Bangladesh), in both English and their countries' main languages. Using JuICE, we find that even the strongest LLM-judge achieves only an F1 of 0.51 in the erroneous span detection task. Furthermore, LLM-judges consistently miss thick cultural errors that local residents readily identify. Our findings suggest that robust cultural evaluation must move beyond surface-level detection toward frameworks that account for the depth and situatedness of cultural meaning.
subject: Computation and Language

title: BioELX: Context-Aware Cross-lingual Biomedical Entity Linking without Task-Specific Supervision
authors: Yi Wang, Corina Dima, Liangyu Zhong, Steffen Staab
summary: Cross-lingual biomedical entity linking (BEL) maps mentions in any language to unique identifiers in a biomedical knowledge base, supporting clinical and biomedical NLP applications. We identify two issues affecting current systems. First, the UMLS (Bodenreider,2004) aliases used to train cross-lingual BEL retrievers are heavily skewed toward English, so retrievers generalize poorly to non-English mentions. Second, although context is often necessary for disambiguation, naively injecting context into retrievers trained only to align aliases severely degrades retrieval. We propose BioELX, a retrieve-rerank framework that addresses both issues. For retrieval, we continue training SapBERT_multi (Liu et al., 2021b) using Wikidata-derived cross-lingual alias supervision, forming shared concept neighborhoods across languages. For reranking, we adapt pretrained LLM rerankers to entity linking through mention-anchored prompting, which marks the target mention so that rerankers score candidates with respect to the intended mention rather than other salient tokens in the context. Experiments show that BioELX achieves new state-of-the-art results on four cross-lingual BEL benchmarks, improving Recall@1 by 4.8 to 18.2 percentage points over prior best results, without any task-specific BEL annotations. Our code and resources are available at https://github.com/AI4MedCode/BioELX.
subject: Computation and Language

title: K-BrowseComp: A Web Browsing Agent Benchmark Grounded in Korean Contexts
authors: Nahyun Lee, Dongkeun Yoon, Guijin Son, Geewook Kim, Dayoon Ko, Jeonghun Park, Haneul Yoo, Jaewon Cho, Junghun Park, Changyoon Lee, Kyochul Jang, Jaeyeon Kim, Eunsu Kim, Woojin Cho, Seungone Kim
summary: Frontier model evaluations are shifting from foundational capabilities (e.g., instruction following and reasoning) toward compositional, agentic ones, but Korean agentic benchmarks remain scarce. We introduce K-BrowseComp, a web-browsing agent benchmark grounded in Korean contexts, consisting of 400 problems. The 300-problem K-BrowseComp-Verified subset is manually constructed and validated by native Korean speakers. On this subset, frontier LLMs, including GPT-5.5, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and GLM-5.1, reach only 30.00--45.67\%, a substantial drop from BrowseComp, while Korean LLMs released through Korea's Proprietary AI Foundation Model program obtain only 0.00--10.33\%. We further construct a 100-problem synthetic split using hard few-shot exemplars and failure-mode-targeted generation to exploit the asymmetry between solving and creating web browsing problems. On the adversarially filtered synthetic diagnostic split, the strongest model reaches only 26.00\%, and we report this split separately as a targeted stress test. We publicly release our data and code.
subject: Computation and Language

title: CARE: A Conformal Safety Layer for Medical Summarization
authors: Suhana Bedi, Bridget Lin, Anson Y. Zhou, Chloe O. Stanwyck, Jenelle A. Jindal, Sanmi Koyejo, David Stutz, Nigam H. Shah
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for medical summarization but can omit medically important information and introduce unsupported claims. Existing error-detection methods produce heuristic or uncalibrated scores, providing no formal control over missed errors and no principled way to trade off safety against clinician review burden.
